title: We Put Childhood Behind a Paywall
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: Kevin Stinehart argues that modern societies have inadvertently made childhood inaccessible through accumulating reasonable decisions—fenced fields, locked playgrounds, removed library chairs, shorter recesses, activities requiring registration and fees. Childhood has ceased to be an environment children naturally inhabit and become something families must privately manufacture, one playdate at a time. This transfer of developmental work onto households is not over-parenting but compensation for what communities no longer provide. It also reproduces inequality rapidly: geography, transportation, adult availability, and income determine which children have the developmental inputs (peer life, unstructured movement, real responsibilities) they need. His 'Tier 0' framework argues schools are investing in increasingly specialized interventions while the universal developmental foundations beneath them—play, belonging, agency, recovery—have been allowed to deteriorate. The solution is structural: children cannot build the environments that build them.
points: No single policy destroys childhood—it is the accumulation of individually reasonable decisions (fenced fields, locked playgrounds, removed seating, shorter recesses) that makes developmental experience inaccessible.
Manufacturing a healthy childhood—coordinating playdates, activities, transportation, and calendars—has become a part-time job transferred from community infrastructure onto individual households.

Once childhood inputs depend on private purchase, inequality expands rapidly: geography, transportation, adult availability, and income determine which children receive the developmental repetitions they need.

Schools are investing in increasingly specialized interventions (Tier 2, Tier 3) while the universal developmental foundation—play, belonging, movement, agency—has been allowed to deteriorate beneath them.

Children cannot fix the deprivation themselves; the solution must be structural—open playgrounds, slower traffic, sidewalks, libraries that welcome young people, and adults willing to accept the noise of childhood.
quotes: A society can inadvertently become hostile to children without ever announcing that children are unwelcome. It happens one reasonable decision at a time.
None of these decisions alone destroys childhood. They simply make it harder to access.
Manufacturing a healthy childhood is now a part-time job for parents.

Architecture determines access. A developmental input that depends on private purchase is not equal - and a childhood that must be privately purchased will reproduce the inequalities of the adult world.
A 30-minute social-skills lesson cannot replace a social world. A poster about resilience cannot compensate for too few encounters with manageable, real-world difficulty.
Children cannot build the environments that build them. That is our job - not because families have failed, but because no family was ever meant to provide an entire world.
